title: Pioneer Factors and Enhancer Looping
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter follows the second half of Lecture 18 of MIT's 7.91J (Foundations of Computational and Systems Biology, Spring 2014, David Gifford): how pioneer transcription factors that open closed chromatin are validated experimentally, and how RNA Pol II ChIA-PET is used to map enhancers to the genes they regulate, including the statistics needed to trust a candidate loop and to estimate how many real events an assay is missing. It assumes familiarity with ChIP-seq/ChIP-qPCR, DNase-seq as a readout of chromatin accessibility, and the hypergeometric and binomial distributions. The computational model that predicts pioneer factors from DNase-seq footprints in the first place — named on the slides only as "Dynamic Bayesian Networks" and "factor binding classification using a log likelihood ratio" — is assumed from earlier in the course and is not developed here; see Sources. ## Chromatin structure has several layers Chromatin's regulatory information is not carried by DNA sequence alone. The lecture organizes it into layers that together place a locus into an "on" (transcriptionally active, open) or "off" (silenced, closed) state: - the DNA sequence itself, and its methylation state, - the positioning of nucleosomes along the DNA, - histone modifications on the proteins the DNA is wrapped around. Chromatin is organized into structural domains built from these layers, and both DNA methylation and chromatin marks carry functional information about a locus's state. That is what makes genome-wide assays of accessibility (DNase-seq) and modification (ChIP-seq) useful proxies for a locus's regulatory state, computationally. ## Pioneer and settler transcription factors The lecture names three computational methods used in this part of the course: Dynamic Bayesian Networks, a log-likelihood-ratio classifier for factor binding, and the hypergeometric distribution. Only the third is worked out on these slides. The first two underlie a model, referred to here as PIQ, that estimates protein occupancy directly from DNase-seq footprints and classifies transcription factors into two functional classes: - **Pioneer factors** bind directly to closed, nucleosome-occupied chromatin and open it. - **Settler factors** require chromatin to already be open — in particular, opened by a pioneer — before they can bind. That distinction, and the claim that losing a pioneer's binding lets chromatin re-close, is what the rest of this section tests experimentally. ## Testing the model with dominant-negative factors A correlation between a predicted pioneer factor's binding sites and open chromatin does not show the factor is causally responsible for opening it. To test causality, Sherwood, Hashimoto and colleagues made dominant-negative (DN) versions of two predicted pioneers, **NFYA** and **Nrf1**, induced them in mouse embryonic stem cells (mES), and measured DNase hypersensitivity (DNase HS) — the standard readout of open chromatin — at each factor's own native binding sites. Inducing DN NFYA or DN Nrf1 reduced DNase HS specifically at that factor's predicted sites ($p < 0.01$), relative to wild-type mES. Because the effect is restricted to the sites of the factor being disrupted, this is evidence that the predicted pioneer is doing causal work: removing its function measurably closes chromatin at the loci it is predicted to act on. A second experiment asks whether the pioneer relationship is directional — does the pioneer open chromatin for a settler, and not the reverse? DN NFYA was induced, and binding of a candidate settler, **c-Myc**, was measured by ChIP-qPCR at two classes of region: "predicted pioneering sites" (where the model predicts NFYA opens chromatin that c-Myc then uses) and "predicted non-pioneering sites." DN NFYA reduced c-Myc's ChIP signal at the predicted pioneering sites but not at the non-pioneering ones ($p < 0.01$). c-Myc's binding depends on NFYA exactly where NFYA is predicted to act as a pioneer, and not elsewhere — that asymmetry is the evidence for a directional, pioneer-then-settler relationship rather than two factors acting independently of one another. ## Pioneer activity is conserved across species The same chromatin-opening effect, summarized per site as a "Chromatin Opening Index," was compared between the mouse ES cell lineage and the human K562 cell line, giving a correlation of $r^2 = 0.84$. Pioneer activity at corresponding sites is conserved between human and mouse — evidence that it reflects an intrinsic property of the factor, not an artifact specific to the mES system used for the dominant-negative experiments. ## Putting the pioneer/settler picture together The lecture summarizes the results so far: - PIQ is highly accurate at predicting transcription factor binding from DNase-seq data. - PIQ can identify pioneer factors that regulate proximal chromatin opening and TF binding. - Certain pioneer TFs are directional, as shown for NFYA and c-Myc. - Settler factors follow pioneer-factor binding, and losing pioneer binding causes chromatin to return to a closed state. That last point is the dynamic form of the state diagram above: a pioneer's binding is not a switch thrown once — it has to be maintained, or the chromatin it opened re-closes. ## Enhancers, looping, and ChIA-PET The lecture's third topic is how distal enhancers regulate genes: not by proximity along the linear DNA sequence, but by physically looping into contact with a promoter. The slides name the players that hold the loop together — an enhancer region, cohesin, the Mediator complex, master-regulator transcription factors, and RNA polymerase II (Pol II), which contacts the target gene's promoter. To find such loops genome-wide, the **ChIA-PET** (Chromatin Interaction Analysis by Paired-End Tag sequencing) protocol immunoprecipitates a specific protein — here, Pol II — then sonicates the crosslinked chromatin and ligates the resulting DNA ends together. Two outcomes are possible: **self-ligation**, where the two ends of a single fragment are rejoined and carry no positional information about looping, and **inter-ligation**, where ends from two different genomic fragments that Pol II had held together are joined — this is the read that reports a loop between two distant genomic positions. The ligation products are then sequenced. ## An example: cell-type-specific looping at Sox2 Applying Pol II ChIA-PET in three cell types — induced motor neurons (iMN), motor neuron progenitors (pMN), and mouse ES cells (mES) — recovers different loop structures at the same locus, the *Sox2* gene. In each cell type, the Pol II loops line up with the ChIP-seq peaks of that cell type's own master regulator: Lhx3 in iMN, Olig2 in pMN, and Sox2 itself in mES. The enhancer wiring of a locus is cell-type-specific, tracking which master regulators are active in that cell type. ## Is a candidate loop real? A hypergeometric test With millions of ligation events genome-wide, some inter-ligation reads linking two particular sites will occur by chance even where there is no real loop. The lecture gives a hypergeometric test for whether an observed linkage is more than that. Let $I_{A,B}$ be the observed number of inter-ligation events linking two binding events (sites) $A$ and $B$. Let $c_A$ and $c_B$ be the total number of ligation-event ends associated with $A$ and with $B$ respectively, and let $N$ be the total number of ligation-event ends genome-wide. The null hypothesis is that every ligation end pairs with any other end with equal probability — no preference for $A$'s ends to land specifically on $B$. Under that null, the number of $A$'s ends that happen to pair with $B$ is exactly the hypergeometric urn problem: draw $c_B$ ends without replacement from a population of $N$, of which $c_A$ are "marked" (belong to $A$), and ask how many marked ends are drawn: $$P(I_{A,B} \mid N, c_A, c_B) = \frac{\binom{c_A}{I_{A,B}}\binom{N - c_A}{c_B - I_{A,B}}}{\binom{N}{c_B}}$$ and the significance of the observed count is the upper-tail probability of seeing at least that many shared ends by chance: $$p = \sum_{i=I_{A,B}}^{\min\{c_A, c_B\}} P(i \mid N, c_A, c_B)$$ A loop between $A$ and $B$ is called real when this $p$-value is small: the observed linkage is far more than random mixing of ligation ends would produce. ## Limitations of ChIA-PET Three issues raised in the lecture: 1. **High false-negative rate.** The libraries produced are not complex enough to find more loops just by sequencing them more deeply — the assay runs out of new information before it runs out of reads. 2. **It is specific to one protein.** The method only sees loops that the immunoprecipitated protein (here, Pol II) takes part in; loops mediated by other machinery are invisible to it. 3. Hi-C and its derivatives, which do not require pulling down a specific protein, "may solve these problems eventually." ## Estimating the true number of events from replicate overlap The hypergeometric distribution reappears for a different question: not "is this specific loop real," but "how many real events actually exist," given two noisy, incomplete replicate measurements of the same underlying population — the same event, whether a binding site or a loop, either is or is not called in a given replicate, so the overlap between two replicates behaves exactly like the urn problem above, with the two replicates' calls playing the role of $c_A$ and $c_B$ and the true (unknown) population size playing the role of $N$. **Worked example.** Two biological replicates of an experiment each detect 1000 events, of which 900 are identical between the replicates. Modeling this as drawing two samples, of sizes $m$ and $n$, from an unknown population of size $N$, and observing an overlap of $k$, the maximum-likelihood estimate of $N$ is the value that makes the observed overlap most probable: $$\hat{N} = \operatorname*{argmax}_N \left[P(X = k; N, m, n)\right]$$ This gives $\hat N \approx 1100$ — noticeably more than either replicate's raw count of 1000, because a population this small would be unlikely to leave roughly 100 events undetected by at least one replicate while still overlapping this heavily. **A closed-form approximation.** For large counts, the hypergeometric distribution for the overlap $X$ is well approximated first by a binomial and then by a normal distribution: $$P(X = k; N, m, n) \approx \text{Binomial}\left(X = k; n = n, p = \frac{m}{N}\right) \approx \text{Normal}\left(X = k; \mu = \frac{mn}{N}, \sigma^2 = \frac{mn}{N}\left(1 - \frac{m}{N}\right)\right)$$ The mean of that normal is $\mu = mn/N$. The observed $k$ is (approximately) most probable when $N$ is chosen so this mean matches the data, $\mu \approx k$, giving the closed form $$\hat{N}(m, n, k) = \frac{mn}{k}$$ Checking this against the worked example: $\hat N = 1000 \times 1000 / 900 \approx 1111$, matching the $\approx 1100$ estimate above. ## Correcting the estimate when some events are false positives If some of the events called in each replicate are false positives, the overlap-based estimator above overestimates $N$: false positives inflate $m$ and $n$ without correspondingly inflating the true overlap $k$. The lecture's correction treats the $k$ shared events as certainly true positives, discounts the remaining, non-shared events in each replicate using a parameter $f$ tied to the assay's true-positive rate (TPR), and then applies the same overlap estimator to the adjusted counts $m'$ and $n'$: $$m' = (1 - f)(m - k) + k, \qquad n' = (1 - f)(n - k) + k$$ **Worked example.** Two replicates of a real experiment gave $m = 3811$ and $n = 1384$ events, with an overlap of $k = 533$. Recomputing $\hat N = m'n'/k$ at several assumed values of the true-positive rate: | TPR | $\hat N$ | | --- | --- | | 0.80 | 7180 | | 0.90 | 8482 | | 1.00 | 9896 | A higher assumed true-positive rate gives a larger estimate of the total number of events for the same observed overlap: trusting the assay more means trusting that its calls unique to one replicate are mostly real too, rather than noise. One consistency check worth flagging: at TPR $= 1$, these numbers reduce to the uncorrected $\hat N = mn/k = 3811 \times 1384 / 533 \approx 9896$, which only happens if $m' = m$ and $n' = n$, i.e. $f = 0$. So the number actually substituted for $f$ in the two update equations behaves like $1 - \text{TPR}$ rather than TPR itself, despite the slide's label. That looseness is inherited from the source (a model-reconstructed slide deck; see Sources) — the argument to take from this section is the shape of the correction, not the letter of the formula: treat the overlap as trustworthy, discount the rest by the assay's error rate, and re-apply the same overlap estimator. ## Sources - All content: MIT OpenCourseWare, 7.91J (Foundations of Computational and Systems Biology, Spring 2014), Lecture 18, "Analysis of Chromatin Structure," David K. Gifford. No transcript, notes, or problem set were supplied for this lecture. - The dominant-negative pioneer-factor experiments (NFYA, Nrf1) and the c-Myc directionality experiment are figures from Sherwood, Richard I., Tatsunori Hashimoto, et al., "Discovery of Directional and Nondirectional Pioneer Transcription Factors by Modeling DNase Profile Magnitude and Shape," *Nature Biotechnology* 32, no. 2 (2014): 171–8, as cited on the slides. The lecture shows results from this paper without reproducing its methods; consult it directly for the underlying PIQ model. - The slides name "Dynamic Bayesian Networks" and "factor binding classification using a log likelihood ratio" as computational methods behind the PIQ pioneer-factor model but do not develop either one on these slides; that material is assumed from earlier in the course and is not part of this chapter. - The converted slide file also contains extracted figures from later pages of the source PDF with no accompanying captions or headings in the conversion; they were not used here, as there is no text anchoring what they show.
